en: And none could tell which was which;
Infidel and Muslim alike
Seethed and filled the place in agitation.
Kökötöy's great riches
Were squandered and scattered;
All the abundant gold
Was trampled underfoot.
Among all those possessions,
Ezkara attacked
The swift horse Maaniker.
Bokmurun, giver of the feast,
Bolted out from among the people;
I saw the place where he fled.
My uncle Koshoy lost his bearings;
I saw the place where he panicked.
There were Muzburchak and Khan Kökchö,
And all the Muslim giants.
There was Akun Khan of Afghanistan,
And all the mighty men.
There was Kökbörü, son of Urumkan,
The lion among heroes.
Unable to withstand anyone,
Before infidels as numerous as cow hairs,
They had a time of reeling in panic.
Sour ayran, blue kurut—
He wrought an end-of-time deed,
Bokmurun, Kökötöy's foul urine,
Trusting in the abundance of gold,
Against the very roots of the Muslim people."
After the boy had spoken thus,
Manas then said:
"Damn your father's grave, young Aydar;
You and Bokmurun are drunk, Aydar!
You have no loyalty, hostile Aydar!
After Khan Kökötöy died
And saw the true world,
Why did you not send word?
At the feast you began, Aydar,
May calamity rise before you, Aydar!
May the masses dig your pit, Aydar;
May dogs tear your flesh, Aydar;
Who would wish to see your face, Aydar!
May Kalmyks eat your head, Aydar;
May infidels eat your feast, Aydar!
Who would listen to your words, Aydar?
Let a single dark night listen, Aydar!
When force came, your chance to come—
Did you not see from the beginning
Beijing where blood was spilled, Aydar?"
Bloodthirsty Manas swelled,
And his thirst for blood seized him.
Flame hissed from his mouth;
With white teeth like a gate,
Your tiger, bloodthirsty Manas,
Gnashed them section by section.
He drew Zulpukor from its sheath;
Young Aydar's face paled and changed,
His forelock spread wide,
And he fell beneath the boy.
As he brought the sword into line,
As he was about to slaughter
Young Aydar with the spreading forelock,
Dear lady Kanykey,
The beauty of the dark-gray people,
The glory of the Muslims—
If you had seen your sister-in-law,
Your mother of surpassing wisdom!
Her white throat trembled,
Her white breast gleamed;
Forty keys in a row
Rang in the pouch at her waist,
And your sister-in-law shone.
Her dawn paled like an argali's,
Her white breast showed;
Before the magnanimous lord,
She spoke softly in sorrow.
Sweet-worded and sharp-eyed,
Fragrant perfume rising, twisting her brass ornaments,
She interceded and begged for his blood.
Her dear quail-like eyes
Shed separate streams of tears;
Her dear currant-black eyes
Shed tears a whip-length long.
Moving gracefully in grief,
Holding him dear,
She pleaded with her lord:
"Can one who is alone strike another alone?
Can striking a lone man prosper?
He is no dark, rugged mountain
That you cannot cross,
No enemy come from the Kalmyks,
No costly crag of a mountain,
No enemy come from China.
What you do is not right;
Please stand without striking him.
If your sword struck the whole age, would it be sated?
If you rend him because he is alone,
Will every hollow in you be filled?
He too is one father's only son;
Can you make him a wretched captive?
Good heavens, can killing a messenger prosper?
If you rend the lone man,
Will your sack be filled by this?"
She poured out many words;
Kanykey grasped the sword,
Her tears spilling.
"Will they not call you witless,
Saying you killed an intercessor?
If the saying is true
That one of seven days is death,
At dawn on the day of Mahshar,
Will they not ride you as a black donkey?
From a gorge with a divided ravine—
My lord, you were the nest's only one.
Were there no racehorse Akkula,
There is no steed to bear and carry you;
Killing an only son is a great shame;
You have no brother to stand shoulder to shoulder with you.
If you do not take the lone man's life,
If you do not extinguish his hearth,
We shall stand watching in sorrow;
Though I am a woman, I ask this."
Kanykey spoke these words,
Standing as an intercessor.
Then, wearing a blue lynx-fur cap,
Wielding a blue-mottled shield,
Foreseeing today
The torment that would come in six months,
His words plain when he spoke,
Saintly Bakay, whose eyes were open,
Who found words in sudden danger
And found sight in darkness,
Good-fortuned when sent ahead,
Like a countless host when sent behind—
The elder stepped between them,
His uncle, saintly Bakay.
Then Bakay said:
"Understand my precious words;
My falcon Manas, heed my tongue.
He is an only son, and so are you;
Do not take the lone man's life,
Do not extinguish his hearth!
Bloodthirsty Manas, my soul's friend,
If you truly are a khan,
Heed what I say
And grant his spoonful of blood!
If you maul the boy,
What you do will be shameful.
Until you go to the great feast,
Until you receive the people's news,
Remain patient.
If you kill one of your own people,
What you do will be tyranny.
In reedy broad Keng-Kol and broad Talas,
You watered the horse Akkula;
Bokmurun acted foolishly,
And you vented your anger here.
You have seen the toll of many lands;
Do not inflict upon the boy
Bokmurun's torment."
Speaking words of many kinds,
His uncle, elder Bakay,
Stepped between them.
Dear lady Kanykey
Pulled the boy out
From beneath the tiger.
The lions Bakay and Kanykey
Saved him from death
And parted them safely.
Tiger Manas roared,
Thundering in wrath:
"The six-edged blade fallen from heaven,
The finest-tempered sword,
Zulpukor, which I myself obtained,
Came to me through the unseen
In the desert of Mediyan.
When facing the enemy
And standing in combat,
It came precisely to me.
When drawn screaming from its sheath,
It never went without drinking blood;
If it did not drink its fill of blood,
It would not return to the sheath.
When Zulpukor came from its sheath,
It had the custom of drinking blood;
When swung, it passed through Karkybar.
The honored sword Zulpukor
Had the worth of a thousand yearling mares.
When drawn roaring from the sheath,
Does your holy man know?
Will Zulpukor, drawn from the sheath,
Go without drinking blood?
When your lord stood swollen in wrath,
The lions Almambet and Chubak,
The forty companions of Khan Manas,
Biting their lips and narrowing their eyes,
Spoke a wondrous word.
Hero Syrgak and servant Shuutu
Flew away like arrows.
Among the Afghan spoil
Were thirty red elephants.
The two heroes Shuutu and Syrgak
Went among the elephants.
Before one could say this or that,
In the blink of an eye,
Khan Manas's red elephants
Had been driven there in a group.
His true thirst for blood seized him;
God struck the bloodthirsty man.
Kanykey and Bakay—
As though he would slaughter them,
He stood avidly.
Bakay sheltered by the khan;
God struck
Young Aydar with the spreading forelock.
When they went among the elephants,
Gray-wolf Manas, the tiger,
Raised Zulpukor in his hand
And struck;
The red elephants before him
Were cut into separate pieces.
Sultan Manas, the tiger,
Watered Zulpukor with blood
And returned it to its sheath.
Making the laugher laugh,
He struck the great war drum,
Announcing that the enemy was coming;
They took the war drum in hand,
Raised the brass mace,
And its champion struck the center.
Ears deafened at its booming,
As though the enemy had come.
Khan Manas's forty nobles—
Each of the forty had a different name,
Famed men who could shatter the age.
The forty wolves entered together
The bloodthirsty hero's treasury.
Your formidable sister-in-law Kanykey
Had prepared
Mighty arrow-proof coats.
All forty companions wrapped themselves in them;
Each of the forty coats was different.
Among those coats
Was the sarinji Almambet would wear;
It bore a letter on its collar
And Almambet's name.
Your sister-in-law Kanykey, the stalwart,
Had made this coat.
Considering her labor,
Its worth equaled an age.
She had its inside tightly lined
And its outside covered at the corners.
She had precious iron riveted to its back;
When spears met, they did not reach flesh,
And it exhausted whoever grappled with its wearer.
She had that coat fitted perfectly
